p: I have read the pages concerning this war more often than any others in the Encyclopaedia, and I have found them harder to bear. It is one thing to write of the sack of Rome or the Black Death; the dead of those calamities have been dead for centuries, and their names are lost. It is another to read of the deaths of the grandsons of men I know, in a war that will begin in thirty-nine years' time, among nations that I have visited and admired, by means of engines that our own engineers are at this moment proudly devising. I shall try to write of it as a historian. I am not sure I shall succeed.

Europe in my own day is kept at peace by a balance among its great powers: Britain, France, the new German Empire proclaimed four years ago in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, Austria-Hungary, Russia, and, more feebly, Italy and the Ottoman Turks. The Encyclopaedia tells me that over the following decades this balance will harden into two armed alliances, Germany with Austria-Hungary on the one side, France with Russia, and later Britain, on the other, each fearful of the other, each building armies and navies of unprecedented size, each with detailed plans for war that, once begun, would move with the speed and rigidity of a railway timetable. The Germans and the British, in particular, will race to build great iron battleships.

On the twenty-eighth of June, nineteen fourteen, the heir to the throne of Austria-Hungary, the Archduke Franz Ferdinand, will be shot dead with his wife in the streets of Sarajevo, in Bosnia, by a young Bosnian Serb nationalist named Gavrilo Princip. Austria, encouraged by Germany, will make demands upon Serbia, which it believed to be behind the murder. Russia will mobilise to protect Serbia. Germany will declare war on Russia and, according to its plan, on France, and to reach France quickly will march through neutral Belgium. Britain, bound by treaty to defend Belgian neutrality, will declare war on Germany on the fourth of August. Within six weeks of a murder in a Balkan town, all the great powers of Europe will be at war. The British Foreign Secretary, Sir Edward Grey, watching the lamps being lit in Whitehall on the eve of the war, will say: the lamps are going out all over Europe; we shall not see them lit again in our lifetime.

Everyone will expect a short war. The Germans will come within some thirty miles of Paris and be stopped at the river Marne. Then both sides will dig in, and within months there will be a line of trenches from the Swiss frontier to the North Sea, which will scarcely move for nearly four years. The weapons of my century, perfected, will make attack almost suicidal: the rifle that fires many shots without reloading, the machine gun, which our own Mr Maxim will invent in a few years and which fires hundreds of bullets a minute, barbed wire, and artillery of immense power. On the first day of the battle of the Somme, the first of July, nineteen sixteen, the British army will lose nearly twenty thousand men killed, the worst day in its history. At Verdun, the French and Germans will lose between them some seven hundred thousand men killed, wounded and missing in ten months, for a few miles of shattered ground. New horrors will be added: poison gas, flame throwers, aeroplanes dropping bombs, the submarine sinking merchant ships without warning, and at last the tank, an iron fort moving on tracks.

The war will spread across the world: to the Turkish fronts at Gallipoli, where Australians and New Zealanders will win undying fame in failure, and in Mesopotamia and Palestine, where, by a strange chance, British soldiers will fight over the ruins of Babylon and enter Jerusalem; to Africa; to the seas. The United States will join in nineteen seventeen. The Germans, exhausted, starved by a British blockade, and their allies collapsing, will ask for an armistice, which will come into force at the eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month of nineteen eighteen. Some nine or ten million soldiers will have died, and millions of civilians. A great epidemic of influenza, spreading in the war's last year, will kill tens of millions more across the world.

The war will destroy four empires: the German, the Austro-Hungarian, the Ottoman and the Russian. The fall of the last will have the greatest consequences. Russia, vast, poor, ruled by an autocratic Tsar and poorly equipped for modern war, will suffer immense losses. In March of nineteen seventeen, strikes and bread riots in the capital, Petrograd, which we know as Saint Petersburg, will turn into revolution when the soldiers refuse to fire on the crowds. Tsar Nicholas the Second will abdicate, and a provisional government will try, without success, to continue the war and to govern. In November of nineteen seventeen, a small and disciplined party of revolutionary socialists, the Bolsheviks, led by Vladimir Ilyich Ulyanov, who calls himself Lenin, a follower of the doctrines of Karl Marx, will seize power in Petrograd. They will make peace with Germany at a heavy price, win a terrible civil war, murder the Tsar and his family in a cellar at Yekaterinburg, and found the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, the first state in the world to be governed according to Marx's teaching. Its promise of a society without classes will inspire millions across the world. Its practice, under Lenin's successor Joseph Stalin, will include the deliberate starvation of peasants, the forced labour camps of Siberia, and the shooting of hundreds of thousands of its own supposed enemies. The Encyclopaedia says that it will last until nineteen ninety-one.

The victors will meet at Paris in nineteen nineteen and draw up the Treaty of Versailles, which will compel Germany to admit responsibility for the war, give up territory and colonies, disarm, and pay enormous reparations. The American President, Woodrow Wilson, will propose a League of Nations to keep the peace for ever, and his own Senate will refuse to join it. The economist John Maynard Keynes, a member of the British delegation, will resign in disgust and predict that a harsh peace will lead to another war. The Encyclopaedia records that he will be right, within twenty years.

They will call it the Great War, and the war to end war. In every town and village of England, there will be a stone monument with the names of the dead. My own village in Shropshire, I have learned, will put up such a stone with twenty-three names upon it. I have looked at the list. I know four of the families.
